title: Streaming backpressure / queue saturation - SRE on-call notes
content:
Quick summary:

- What happened: Between ~2026-04-20T09:14:00Z and 2026-04-20T10:05:00Z the hosted streaming API experienced elevated 5xx rates and end-to-end tail latency spikes for a subset of customers using long-lived streaming sessions. The primary symptom was steady growth in the streaming request-handling queue on edge muxers and a cascade of HTTP 502/504 from downstream worker pools.

- Impact: ~4.2% of production streaming requests returned 5xx during the window, with tail latency P99s for streaming endpoints increasing from ~120ms to ~2.1s for affected regions (us-west-2). A small number of clients saw session disconnects and had to reconnect. No data loss reported; sessions that reconnected resumed normally.

- Detection: Alert: STREAMING_WORKER_QUEUE_DEPTH_HIGH (threshold 1500 msgs) fired at 2026-04-20T09:16:18Z. Follow-up alert STREAMING_PROXY_5XX_RATE_HIGH (5xx > 1%) fired at 09:18:02Z. On-call paged at 09:19.

Timeline (UTC):
- 09:14:00 - first abnormal increase in muxer queue length observed on dashboards (manual exploration by monitoring runbook).
- 09:16:18 - automated alert STREAMING_WORKER_QUEUE_DEPTH_HIGH triggered for us-west-2.
- 09:18:02 - 5xx rate crossed automated threshold. Slack thread created (#incident-streaming).
- 09:20:00 - first mitigation: increased worker_pool size by +25% via autoscaler override (temporary). Partial reduction in queue growth but 5xx persisted.
- 09:28:00 - discovered a correlation: sudden spike in small short-lived reroute requests from a single customer tenant ID (tenant-x) with many concurrent streaming sessions opening and immediately sending high-frequency messages.
- 09:35:00 - enabled per-tenant soft-rate limit on open streaming session creation for tenant-x (throttle to 50 new sessions / minute). Queue growth stabilized.
- 09:45:00 - rolling restart of streaming-proxy pods to clear transient backlog of stalled connections. Short blips of connection reset observed but overall 5xx rate trended down.
- 10:05:00 - incident declared mitigated; monitoring observed normal queue depths and 5xx returned to baseline by 10:12:00.

Initial root cause hypothesis:
- The immediate cause was an unbounded burst of streaming session creations + high message fanout from a single tenant that overloaded the muxer->worker queue coupling. Two amplifiers made the effect worse: (1) an overly permissive per-connection concurrency policy in the edge muxer that allowed many ephemeral sessions to occupy internal buffers; (2) degraded KV cache lookup performance (seen as higher KV latency) causing workers to spend more CPU/latency per message, reducing throughput and increasing queue dwell time.

Evidence supporting hypothesis:
- Grafana: muxer queue depth correlated closely with tenant-x session creation rate (annotation + correlation panel).
- Traces: distributed tracing shows increased time in kv-cache.get (P95 from ~1.6ms to ~12ms) for requests during the window.
- Worker metrics: worker-side CPU increased ~30% and message processing time per-message doubled for affected shards.
- Logs: streaming-proxy logs show many ephemeral connections with small payloads and frequent open/close pattern from the same IP block owned by tenant-x.

Why it became P0-level:
- Existing soft limits for session creation were tuned for steady-growth patterns, not pathological rapid open/close loops.
- Autoscaler for workers reacts to CPU/latency slowly; autoscaling alone cannot prevent queue overflow when processing cost per-message increases sharply.

Immediate mitigations taken (chronological):
1) Manual temporary increase of worker pool capacity (+25%) via aws/gke override to buy time. (Benji)
2) Per-tenant throttle applied to tenant-x streaming session creation (soft-limit, rejected new sessions with 429 until stabilised). (Aisha)
3) Rolling restart of streaming-proxy pods to drop stuck socket state and reduce OS-level connection fanout. (Carlos)
4) Short-term configuration: reduced muxer per-connection buffer retention to 30s (from 2m) to free up memory and queue slots. (Zoe)

Commands & links used during troubleshooting (notes to self):
- kubectl -n streaming get hpa -o wide; kubectl -n streaming scale deployment/streaming-worker --replicas=24
- curl -X POST "https://controlplane.redwood/api/v1/tenants/tenant-x/throttle" -d '{"streaming_new_session_rate":50}'  # temp
- grafana dashboards: streaming/muxer-queues, streaming/worker-latency (use correlation view)
- traces: jaeger/service=streaming-proxy?start=2026-04-20T09:00

Permanent root cause analysis (consolidated):
- Trigger: tenant-x load generator (malfunctioning integration) created many short sessions that produced high fanout and heavy KV cache traffic.
- Amplifier 1: muxer allowed unlimited ephemeral sessions to allocate internal resources (buffers/slots), leading to queue backlog.
- Amplifier 2: KV cache SLO regression during the window (disk/ephemeral node GC on one kv-cluster shard) slowed down worker-side lookups and increased per-message processing time.
- System design gap: lack of effective per-tenant open-session rate limiting and insufficient backpressure propagation from workers to proxies/muxers. Also, autoscaler is reactive and too slow for sudden bursts when processing cost per unit increases.

Proposed runbook changes (draft):
- Add a new incident play: "Streaming: tenant surge/backpressure" with clear steps:
  * Detect: runbook should include tenant-level session-open rate panel and an alert STREAMING_TENANT_SESSION_OPEN_HIGH (per-tenant threshold: 100/min by default).
  * Immediate actions: apply per-tenant soft-throttle (controlplane API) -> if that fails, apply tenant blackhole gate for extreme cases (ops only).
  * If queue depth > X and 5xx > Y, scale worker_pool to N and trigger rolling restart of streaming-proxy in a controlled fashion (30s drain, one AZ at a time).
  * If kv-cache P95 > 10ms, switch the worker-side cache to read-through fallback mode (local LRU) and escalate kv-cluster runbook.
- Implement backpressure channel: worker should surface processing backpressure metrics to proxy (gRPC headers or health flags) so proxy can immediately start rejecting new sessions instead of relying on global queue depth alerts.
- Tune defaults: reduce per-connection buffer retention (default 120s -> 45s) and set a hard cap of 10k ephemeral sessions per-proxy instance.
- Autoscaler tuning: add a burst-mode that can temporarily oversubscribe more aggressively when processing latency increases and queue depth is rapidly rising.

Action items (owners + ETA):
- Implement per-tenant session-open alert and controlplane throttle endpoint hardening (owner: product-hosted-api backend team; owner alias: Priya Shah). ETA: 2026-05-10.
- Instrument worker->proxy backpressure header and gating logic (owner: serving-runtime team; Benji Park). ETA: 2026-05-03.
- Run KV cluster health sweep and fix identified shard causing GC pauses (owner: infra-kv; Carlos Mendes). ETA: 2026-04-27.
- Update streaming runbook with new play and put it under on-call rotation docs (owner: eng-sre; Aisha Khan). ETA: 2026-04-30.
- Add automated chaos test that simulates tenant-level short-session bursts to exercise backpressure and autoscaler (owner: release-engineering + qa; Zoe Li). ETA: 2026-05-17.

Open questions & follow-ups: (for product / security review)
- Is it safe to expose per-tenant throttle controls in the control plane API (audit / RBAC implications)? Need security review.
- Should we proactively notify customers when we apply tenant-level throttles, and what is the expected support flow?
- Are there performance regressions in the kv-cache rollout in the last week? (check deploy window 2026-04-18).

Appendix - quick metrics snapshots (copy to final postmortem):
- Peak STREAMING_WORKER_QUEUE_DEPTH (us-west-2): 18,200 at 09:21:13Z
- 5xx rate peak (streaming endpoints): 4.2% at 09:19:40Z
- KV cache P95 at peak window: 12.6ms (baseline P95: 1.6ms)
- Worker CPU delta (baseline -> peak): +31%

Notes to reviewer:
- This is an in-progress draft; I intentionally left command snippets and direct controlplane links so on-call can reproduce mitigation quickly. We should sanitize any customer-identifying details before final postmortem publication.
- Suggest we run a short post-incident blameless review with tenant-x integration leads to understand client-side behavior.

End of notes.
